name: Bruxism
preview_text: In TCM, teeth grinding is a language your body speaks - the timing, triggers, and accompanying symptoms point to which organ system needs attention. With the right pattern diagnosi...
synonyms: ["Excessive Tooth Grinding", "Teeth Grinding", "Bruxism Teeth", "teeth grinding during sleep", "Clenching or grinding teeth at night", "Grinding of teeth", "Grinding teeth during sleep", "Clenching Of Teeth", "Clenching Of The Jaw", "Clenching Teeth", "Clenched Jaw"]
conventional_description: Bruxism is the medical term for involuntary grinding or clenching of the teeth, most often during sleep. It can cause tooth wear, jaw pain, headaches, and disrupted sleep. While the exact cause isn't always clear, it's commonly linked to stress, anxiety, sleep disorders, or an abnormal bite. Diagnosis is usually made by a dentist based on tooth wear patterns and symptoms, and sometimes confirmed with a sleep study.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments focus on protecting the teeth and reducing muscle activity. A custom-fitted mouth guard or splint is the most common approach. Stress management techniques, muscle relaxants, and in some cases Botox injections into the jaw muscles may also be recommended. If an underlying sleep disorder or medication side effect is identified, addressing that may help.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands teeth grinding as a sign that something is disturbing the smooth flow of Qi and Blood to the jaw. The Liver and Stomach are often the key players. The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi and is easily upset by stress; when Qi stagnates, it can generate heat that rises along the channels to the jaw, causing tension and involuntary clenching. The Stomach channel runs directly to the teeth and gums, so dietary heat or inflammation can also travel upward and trigger grinding.
But the root cause isn't always heat. When the Spleen and Heart are weak from overwork or poor diet, the body lacks the nourishment to calm the muscles and the mind at night. This deficiency pattern leads to restless sleep and grinding from a different mechanism - not excess, but emptiness. In some cases, Phlegm and Heat combine to create a sticky obstruction that disturbs sleep, while long-standing Yin deficiency can cause empty heat to flare upward and tighten the sinews.
That's why the same grinding symptom can arise from such different internal landscapes. A stressed executive with a red face and bitter taste has a very different TCM diagnosis than an exhausted new mother with pale skin and poor appetite, even if both grind their teeth at night. TCM's strength is its ability to identify the underlying pattern and treat it accordingly.
classical_translation: "When heat qi is exuberant, there is grinding of the teeth."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about your emotional life and daily stressors. If the grinding flares during tense periods and comes with irritability, a bitter taste, or tension headaches, the pattern is often Liver Qi Stagnation that has turned into Heat. The tongue is red, especially at the sides, with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse feels wiry and rapid - signs of constrained Qi that has overheated and risen to the jaw.
When the grinding is linked to rich, spicy, or greasy meals, Stomach Fire is the likely culprit. You may also notice bad breath, swollen or bleeding gums, and a constant thirst for cold drinks. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery, reflecting the excess heat churning inside the stomach and travelling up its channel to the teeth.
If the grinding happens alongside mental fog, poor appetite, and restless sleep with vivid dreams, Heart and Spleen Deficiency may be at play. This pattern often arises from overthinking and irregular eating. The tongue looks pale and puffy with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and thready - the body lacks the nourishment needed to soothe the muscles and calm the mind at night.
Phlegm-Heat produces a heavy, stuck sensation: you might wake with a sticky taste, have phlegm in the throat, and feel mentally foggy. The tongue is red with a thick, greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is slippery and rapid. The turbid phlegm combines with heat to agitate the spirit and block the channels, leading to involuntary jaw clenching during sleep.
Empty-Heat from Yin Deficiency often appears after long-term overwork or late nights. The grinding is accompanied by a dry mouth at night, warm palms and soles, and a floating feeling of heat. The tongue is red with little or no coating, and the pulse is fine and rapid. Here the body’s cooling fluids are depleted, allowing a low-grade heat to dry the sinews and trigger grinding.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation that transforms into Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["Grinding or clenching worse with stress and anger", "Irritability and explosive anger", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Distending or burning pain along the ribs", "Headache at the temples", "Red face and eyes"]
patterns.worse_with: Anger and frustration, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol and coffee, Late nights and overwork
patterns.better_with: Stress reduction, Cooling foods and drinks, Gentle exercise, Regular sleep schedule
patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress and frustration cause the Liver’s Qi to become stuck. Over time, that stuck Qi generates heat, which rises upward along the Liver and Gallbladder channels. This heat travels to the jaw, tightening the sinews and triggering involuntary clenching and grinding, especially during sleep when the mind is less able to restrain the restless Qi.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides and a yellow coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid, especially at the left middle (Liver) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and emotional stress are the root cause of Liver Qi stagnation in this pattern, so they directly fuel the heat that rises to the jaw. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add more heat to the body, making the upward flare even stronger. Cooling foods and stress-reducing activities help soothe the Liver, clear heat, and prevent Qi from surging upward, which eases the tension in the jaw muscles.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize stress management through gentle exercise like walking or yoga, and aim for a consistent bedtime routine. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat and irritate the Liver. Cooling foods like cucumber, celery, and chrysanthemum tea can help soothe internal heat.

patterns.why_this_happens: Excess heat builds up in the Stomach, often from a diet heavy in spicy, greasy, or fried foods. The Stomach channel runs directly to the gums and teeth, so this fire rises along the channel, creating tension and involuntary contraction in the jaw muscles. At night, the heat disturbs the mind and the muscles, leading to loud grinding and clenching.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, often with central prickles, thick dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò), slippery (滑 huá), and forceful, especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy and greasy foods directly generate Stomach Heat, which rises along the channel to the teeth and jaw, triggering grinding. Late-night eating forces the Stomach to work when it should be resting, creating excess heat that disturbs sleep and muscle relaxation. Cooling foods and drinks clear this heat and soothe the Stomach, while a calm mind and settled stomach prevent the upward surge of fire that tenses the jaw.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat. Eat more cooling, moistening foods like cucumber, watermelon, and steamed leafy greens. Chew slowly and stop eating at least two hours before bed to allow the Stomach to settle. Gentle jaw stretches before sleep can help release tension.

patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, the Spleen produces Qi and Blood from food, while the Heart houses the mind (Shen) and governs blood circulation. Overthinking and irregular eating weaken the Spleen, leading to a shortage of Qi and Blood. This means the jaw muscles-governed by the Spleen-lose their nourishment, and the Heart cannot anchor the mind during sleep. The result is restless sleep with involuntary clenching and grinding, as the unsettled spirit and undernourished muscles fail to relax.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, tender body with teeth marks; thin white coating. Pulse: Fine and weak, especially at the Heart (left cun) and Spleen (right guan) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overthinking and irregular eating deplete the Spleen and Heart, which are the root of this pattern. Warm, nourishing foods and rest rebuild Qi and Blood, while cold and raw foods further weaken the Spleen. Mental strain directly harms the Heart and Spleen, so calming the mind and reducing stress are essential to stop the grinding.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible meals like congee, soups, and stewed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Prioritize regular sleep and rest, and engage in gentle movement like walking or tai chi. Reduce mental strain and overthinking, and consider meditation or deep breathing to calm the mind before bed.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Phlegm and Heat combine, they create a sticky, turbulent obstruction that disturbs the Heart and unsettles the mind. This internal agitation leads to restless sleep, and the Heat rises along the Stomach channel to the jaw, causing involuntary clenching and grinding. The Phlegm component makes the sensation heavy and sticky, often leaving a feeling of something lodged in the throat or chest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red and slightly swollen with a thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò), like beads rolling under the finger.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy and rich foods directly generate the Phlegm and Dampness that combine with Heat to disturb the mind. Alcohol and sweets add more Heat, while late meals leave undigested food to stagnate into Phlegm overnight. Cooling, light foods and gentle movement help the body clear Phlegm and drain Heat, calming the mind and releasing the jaw.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, sweet, and dairy-rich foods that create Phlegm. Eat light, cooling meals with plenty of cooked vegetables. A short walk after dinner helps Qi move and prevents Phlegm from forming overnight.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's cooling and nourishing Yin fluids run low over a long period, empty heat flares upward because there is not enough Yin to anchor it. This heat rises along the channels to the jaw, drying the sinews and making them tight and irritable, which triggers involuntary grinding and clenching during sleep. The grinding is almost always worse at night, when Yin energy should be most active but is depleted, and it comes with classic signs of Yin deficiency like a dry mouth, night sweats, and a restless, unrefreshing sleep.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with cracks and little or no coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid, weak on deep pressure, especially at the left rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin deficiency means the body's cooling, moistening reserves are already low. Late nights, overwork, and stress burn up even more Yin, while spicy food and alcohol create extra heat, making the empty fire flare higher. Rest, early nights, and moistening foods help conserve and rebuild Yin, while cool, calm surroundings prevent the heat from rising to the jaw. This is why simple habits like going to bed early and eating pears can make a real difference - they directly support the body's ability to anchor heat and keep sinews relaxed.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritise rest and a regular sleep schedule - going to bed by 10:30pm helps preserve Yin. Eat moistening, cooling foods like pear, lily bulb, snow fungus, black sesame, and congee; avoid spicy, greasy, or overly roasted foods that consume fluids. Keep alcohol and coffee to a minimum. Gentle evening practices like yin yoga or meditation can calm the mind and prevent the restless heat that triggers grinding.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture stop teeth grinding?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can help reduce the frequency and intensity of teeth grinding by relaxing the jaw muscles and calming the nervous system. It works best when combined with herbal formulas that address the underlying pattern. Most patients notice less tension after a few sessions, though lasting change requires consistent treatment over several weeks.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to work for bruxism?
faqs.answer: Many people notice less jaw tension and better sleep within 2-4 weeks of starting herbs. Excess patterns like Liver Heat or Stomach Fire often respond faster, while deficiency patterns may need 3-6 months to fully rebuild the body's reserves. Consistency is key - herbs are typically taken daily, and your practitioner will adjust the formula as you improve.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role, especially if your grinding is linked to Stomach Heat. Avoiding spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as late-night heavy meals, can reduce heat and inflammation. Eating more cooling foods like cucumber, pear, and congee, and avoiding stimulants like coffee, can support your treatment.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use Chinese herbs with a mouth guard?
faqs.answer: Yes, there is no interaction. The mouth guard protects your teeth while herbs work internally to reduce grinding. Always inform your dentist and TCM practitioner about all treatments you are using.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with daytime clenching too?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Daytime clenching is often linked to stress and Liver Qi stagnation. TCM treats the root cause, so both daytime and nighttime grinding can improve. Acupuncture and herbs that smooth Liver Qi and clear heat are particularly helpful.

faqs.question: Will the grinding come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: If the underlying imbalance is fully corrected, grinding may not return. However, if the same triggers - chronic stress, poor diet, or overwork - resume, symptoms can recur. Your practitioner will teach you lifestyle habits to maintain balance and prevent relapse.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with teeth grinding?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture and gentle herbal formulas can be used for children, often with excellent results. Pediatric dosages are adjusted, and non-needle techniques like acupressure or ear seeds are also effective. Always consult a qualified TCM practitioner experienced in treating children.

research.title: Efficacy Observation of Auricular Point Pressing Combined with Five Element Music for Bruxism
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 90 patients with nocturnal bruxism. The combination of auricular point pressing and five-element music therapy achieved an 86.7% total effective rate, significantly outperforming either therapy alone (46.7% and 50.0%). The combined group also showed greater improvements in anxiety, depression, sleep quality, and quality of life scores.
research.periodical: Shi XL, Su ZY, Chen J, Jia XH. Efficacy Observation of Auricular Point Pressing Combined with Five Element Music for Bruxism. Shanghai Journal of Acupuncture and Moxibustion. 2022;41(3):225-230.
